Other Macs

Use GateFox across several Macs: share one Mac's accounts with others, or work on another Mac over SSH from the Codex app or the Claude app.

About 7 min read · 4 sections

On this page
01 Share one Mac's accounts 02 Work on another Mac over SSH 03 A separate Codex CLI home 04 Details

There are two separate things you may want, and they combine:

Goal How Who runs the model call
Use the main Mac's accounts on a laptop The laptop gets a client token and a tunnel The main Mac's gateway
Work in a project on another Mac (files, terminal, tools there) Codex app: SSH connection · Claude app: SSH environment See below

Share one Mac's accounts

Keep every account on one Mac. Each other Mac gets only a client token and an SSH tunnel; no account credentials are copied. On the other Mac, after installing GateFox:

umask 077; mkdir -p ~/.local/state/gatefox-client
ssh you@main-mac 'gateway token' > ~/.local/state/gatefox-client/client-token
gateway setup --client --port 3459 --token-file ~/.local/state/gatefox-client/client-token
gateway tunnel install --tunnel-id main --host you@main-mac --port 3459 --remote-port 3457
gateway desktop register && gateway doctor

The tunnel runs inside the existing GateFox service; nothing else starts at login. The client token unlocks every account on the main Mac, so keep it owner-only and give it only to your own devices. The main Mac must stay awake and reachable.

Model selection stays on the main Mac: run gateway discover … --load there, and every client sees the change.

Work on another Mac over SSH

In both apps the chat stays in this Mac's window, while files, the terminal and tools run on the other Mac (the host).

Codex app Claude app
On the host GateFox and the Codex CLI, then gateway ssh register Nothing; no GateFox needed
On this Mac Nothing beyond SSH tailnetListener and configure --direct --tailnet --ssh-host …
Add the host in the app The app's SSH connection settings, by the alias from ~/.ssh/config New environment → SSH → Add SSH connection…
Which gateway answers The host's own gateway This Mac's gateway, over Tailscale HTTPS
Network SSH SSH, plus Tailscale with HTTPS Certificates on

1. Make ssh HOST work (both apps)

Both apps use your normal OpenSSH setup, so get a password-free login working in a terminal first. With Tailscale on both Macs, use the host's Tailscale address:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_studio       # once, no passphrase or one in your agent
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_studio.pub edi@100.124.102.126

Then give it a short name in ~/.ssh/config:

Host studio
  HostName 100.124.102.126
  User edi
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_studio
  IdentitiesOnly yes

ssh studio hostname must print the host's name without asking for anything. Accept its host key there once.

2a. Codex app

On the host, install GateFox (the setup) and the Codex CLI, connect its accounts, then route the Codex command through the gateway:

gateway ssh register --codex "$(command -v codex)"
gateway ssh status        # {"registered":true,"command":"…/.local/bin/codex"}

--codex names the original Codex CLI; GateFox puts a managed ~/.local/bin/codex in front of it, which must come first on the host's PATH for SSH logins. On this Mac, add studio in the Codex app's SSH connection settings and open a project there. Its picker shows the models of the host's gateway. A host that should use another Mac's accounts is a client of that Mac (above).

2b. Claude app

On this Mac, with the Claude app quit:

# once: "tailnetListener": true in this Mac's gateway configuration
gateway claude-desktop configure --direct --tailnet \
  --ssh-host studio --ssh-host 100.124.102.126 --apply

List both the alias and the address it resolves to (ssh -G studio | grep '^hostname'). Open the Claude app → New environment → SSH → Add SSH connection…, enter Host studio, your user and the IdentityFile, pick a folder and create the environment. See Claude app SSH environments for the errors you may see.

Example: three Macs

MacBook (own accounts)        Studio (own accounts)        macbook-server
──────────────────────        ─────────────────────        ──────────────────────
Codex app  ══SSH═════════════════════════════════════════► GateFox + Codex CLI
Claude app ══SSH═════════════════════════════════════════► nothing to install
   └─ model calls ◄── Tailscale HTTPS ─────────────────────┘
Claude app ══SSH══════════════► Studio

Repeat step 1 for every pair of Macs you connect, and step 2 for each app you use. A client-only Mac (shared accounts) works in both apps locally and for Codex over SSH, but cannot serve Claude app SSH sessions: tailnetListener needs a gateway with its own accounts.

A separate Codex CLI home

To try gateway models in the Codex CLI without touching your main settings, generate a complete configuration in its own home:

mkdir -p ~/.config/gatefox/clients/codex
gateway codex-config --model codex/gpt-6.1-sol > ~/.config/gatefox/clients/codex/config.toml
CODEX_HOME=~/.config/gatefox/clients/codex codex

On a client-only Mac add --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:3459/v1 --token-file ~/.local/state/gatefox-client/client-token. The command saves a public catalog next to the token; run it again after the main Mac changes its model selection. The Codex client owns its workspace and runs tools locally; moving inference to another Mac does not move file edits there.

Details

For the desktop adapter, set the client configuration port to the forwarded loopback port. Use an absolute client state directory containing the private client-token file. The adapter fetches fresh public metadata from the inference host, so it does not need provider credentials or a local account discovery run. CLI profile catalogs remain startup snapshots.

Installed clients can use a configuration without local providers:

gateway setup --client --port 3459 --token-file ./client-token
gateway tunnel install --tunnel-id host --host user@host \
  --port 3459 --remote-port 3457
gateway doctor
gateway desktop register

Copy the client token through authenticated SSH with owner-only permissions. gateway doctor verifies the forwarded public catalog. Each device needs its own desktop registration; syncing a chat does not register its model provider. The native control panel shows this client-only configuration as a read-only shared catalog and identifies the serving host through authenticated GET /v1/gateway-info. An older host without that endpoint must be updated to show its catalog in the control panel; inference and the existing model endpoint are unchanged. Connection and model-selection editing stays on the host. Register the backend that owns the chat's workspace. Sharing the catalog does not transfer local workspace files or automatically configure an SSH execution backend that bypasses the desktop adapter.

For desktop SSH projects in the Codex app, run gateway ssh register --codex ORIGINAL_PATH on the remote Mac. Then add its existing host alias under the client's SSH connection settings. Those rows are native SSH connections: the desktop runs Codex on the remote Mac, so the gateway models available in them come from that Mac's own gateway ssh register and gateway configuration, not from the client's catalog. The gateway listener on that Mac follows installs by itself: the first connection made after an update starts a listener on the new release, and any session already running finishes on the old one. Only the listener owns upgrade retirement for Unix sessions. A session cannot upgrade its containing process by disconnecting: reconnecting its native proxy would return to that same loaded listener. Per-session idle upgrade watches are therefore reserved for stdio adapters, whose parent actually starts a new process. Managed listeners retire when no sessions remain, or an installed-release bootstrap publishes a replacement alias without terminating existing sessions.

For drop diagnosis, correlate client connection-state timestamps with the remote unix_session_end telemetry record. It includes a process-local sessionId, fixed cause, numeric WebSocket closeCode, and durationMs. Causes distinguish local session end/failure, listener shutdown, queue/protocol limits, socket errors, and an otherwise unclassified transport close. A transport_closed/1006 record alone does not prove a Wi-Fi, SSH, or peer fault; it requires client-side evidence. No close reason, exception text, address, RPC body, or tool arguments are logged. gateway diagnostics --since 1 groups them under connectionEnds by cause and close code; use the underlying event timestamps to correlate both ends. After a reboot, it also recovers its own dead socket when macOS has changed the filesystem device number. See automatic reboot recovery for ownership checks and the separate desktop-startup boundary.

On macOS, the SSH proxy gives the original Codex byte copier fresh stdout and stderr pipes. Node forwards their opaque bytes with backpressure and waits for output to drain before returning the native exit status. Inheriting a descriptor Node already made nonblocking could make the native copier fail with Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 35) when its output filled, producing an abnormal WebSocket close even though the listener and shared engines survived. The regression pauses the caller while the real signed native proxy sends a 4 MiB stream, then verifies every byte and its successful exit. No protocol frames, tool calls or reconnects are replayed by this forwarding. The app's Unix socket and native proxy must reach the gateway adapter on that machine; the built-in Control other devices connection currently bypasses it. See the adapter setup for command protection and removal.
